steps.title: One client, four people
steps.body: This app holds ONE confidential client. Every read and every write names the person it acts for (acting_as), and the engine answers as that person. The app filters nothing itself: no WHERE clause anywhere decides who sees what.

steps.title: Roles are relations
steps.body: Alice owns Website Relaunch and Hiring Plan and is a member of Mobile App. Owner, manager, member and viewer are four relations from Project to User, and each one carries a guard in the model.

steps.title: Who can do what
steps.body: Open the overview: the same query, run once as each person.

steps.title: Same query, four answers
steps.body: Each row is that person's own read, through the same client. Bob never sees Hiring Plan; for him it does not exist. Diana reads one project, as a viewer, and one task elsewhere: it is assigned to her.

steps.title: The guards, in words
steps.body: Owners may do everything, managers everything but delete the project, members read everything and change only their own tasks, viewers only read. And anyone may change a task assigned to them, even in a project they cannot open.

steps.title: Now be Charlie
steps.body: Charlie is a member of Website Relaunch: he reads every task in it, and may change only the ones assigned to him.

steps.title: Same buttons, different answers
steps.html: Move Bob's Write the launch announcement: the engine refuses, ROW_FORBIDDEN · iam. Then move Migrate the blog, which is Charlie's: it goes through. Nothing is hidden or disabled in the page; the answer comes from the guards.

steps.title: Adding a task writes the project
steps.body: Try adding one. A task is added through its project, so the project's guard decides, and a member may only read the project. Owners and managers may.

steps.title: Who may change who is in
steps.body: Try adding Diana as a member. Refused for the same reason: the people of a project are its links, and only its owner and managers may write them.

steps.title: Bob, the manager
steps.body: Open Bob's window. He manages Website Relaunch: he may add, assign and delete its tasks, but not delete the project. Keep both windows where you can see them.

steps.title: Notifications that cannot leak
steps.html: In Bob's window, assign Fix the contact form to Charlie. A notification arrives here, the bell counts it and so does the tab title. The app is told only that something changed; it reads again as Charlie and writes the notification from the difference, so it can never name a row Charlie may not read.

steps.title: Diana, the viewer
steps.body: Open Diana's window. She reads Website Relaunch and can change none of it. Under 'Projects you can't open' she has one task in Mobile App: the task's assignee guard lets her in, the project's guards keep the project out.

steps.title: Same SQL, different numbers
steps.body: One SQL template for everyone. The engine injects the task guards into it, so each person counts only what they may read: Charlie sees less of Alice's work than Alice does.

steps.title: The guards live in the model
steps.body: Project and Project Task carry every rule you just met: four role relations on Project, the same four reached through the project on Project Task, and the assignee. They ship with the model and apply to any client, this one included.

workspaces.title: The data layer is this file
workspaces.html: This tab is project.xsql: projects with their people, tasks, and the workload SQL. go generate turned it into the typed Go API the app calls, the Overview batch included. Run one and you get exactly what the page gets, as the user you signed in as.
